description: Ground-truth vulnerability list for the lib.rs (Anchor lending) eval fixture. A finding 'counts' as matching one of these only if it identifies the same location AND the same underlying issue. Use with evals/evals.json eval #2 and EVAL-METHODOLOGY.md's Layer 3 scoring.

vulnerabilities.description: There is no per-user deposit record anywhere in this program, and withdraw() never checks the caller-supplied `amount` against anything the caller actually deposited. Any signer can call withdraw with an arbitrary amount up to pool_vault's full lamport balance and drain it, since the only account required is a valid Signer, not proof of having deposited that amount.
vulnerabilities.why_planted: The most severe finding — a real fund-drain, and one that's easy to miss if an audit only checks Solana's classic signer/owner-check categories (which are technically satisfied here — `user` IS correctly a Signer) without also checking whether business logic actually authorizes the amount. Tests whether the audit goes beyond the sealevel-attacks checklist mechanics into what the checklist's own 'Coverage traceability' section calls out as beyond-canonical-list territory.

verified.method: Confirmed by inspection: withdraw()'s Accounts struct requires only Signer<'info> for `user`, with no per-user deposit-record account in scope at all — there is no account the instruction could check a balance against even if it wanted to. This is directly readable from the account struct, not merely inferred.

fail_to_pass.description: LiteSVM unit test: attacker who never deposited anything calls withdraw() for an amount equal to the full pool_vault balance. Tests the REAL invariant — attacker's lamport balance actually increased by stolen funds — not just 'did the instruction return Ok', per the SWE-ABS lesson.
fail_to_pass.expected_before_fix: FAILS — the instruction succeeds (LiteSVM's send_transaction returns Ok) and the attacker's balance increases by the stolen amount, even though no signer/owner check was technically violated.
fail_to_pass.expected_after_fix: PASSES once withdraw() requires and checks a per-user deposit-record account (e.g. a PDA seeded by [b"deposit", user.key()]) and rejects amount > recorded balance — the transaction should then fail for an attacker with no deposit record.

vulnerabilities.pass_to_pass: An honest depositor withdrawing an amount they actually deposited must continue to succeed and receive exactly that amount after any fix — a fix that blocks all withdrawals (e.g. removing the instruction) is not an acceptable fix.

vulnerabilities.category: Account data matching / PDA misuse — unvalidated pool_vault
vulnerabilities.location: Deposit and Withdraw account structs, lines 67-69 and 78-80
vulnerabilities.description: pool_vault is typed as a raw AccountInfo with only a `#[account(mut)]` constraint — no seeds/bump tying it to this specific pool, and no owner check. A caller can pass an arbitrary account as pool_vault in either deposit or withdraw, directing funds to/from an unrelated account rather than this pool's actual vault.
vulnerabilities.why_planted: Directly exercises Sealevel Attacks category #1 (account data matching) and #7/#8 (bump seed canonicalization / PDA sharing) — added to the checklist specifically after the external review found these were missing as standalone items; this fixture is what should catch a regression if that checklist coverage is ever weakened.

vulnerabilities.description: Raw `-=` rather than `checked_sub`, unlike deposit() which correctly uses `checked_add` (line 42) — inconsistent arithmetic discipline within the same file. Given LEND-1's lack of a balance check, this can underflow if amount exceeds total_deposits, which Anchor/Rust will panic on in a debug build but could behave differently depending on the release/overflow-checks configuration — either way, an explicit checked_sub with a proper error is the correct pattern, matching what deposit() already does correctly.
vulnerabilities.why_planted: Tests whether an audit that already caught LEND-1 also catches the secondary, related-but-distinct arithmetic issue rather than stopping at the first finding in a function.

not_a_vulnerability_but_might_be_flagged.note: Missing signer check is NOT the right category for LEND-1, even though it's the program's most severe issue — `user` is correctly typed as Signer<'info> throughout. A finding that mislabels LEND-1 as 'missing signer check' rather than 'missing balance/authorization check' should be scored as a near-miss (right severity, wrong category) not a full match.
